strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear demonstration that existing skill-based meta-RL methods (SiMPL, SPiRL) degrade significantly with noisy demonstrations, addressing an under-explored but practically relevant challenge
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 4 environments, multiple noise levels, 7 baselines, consistent improvements especially at high noise levels (e.g., Office σ=0.3: 1.68 vs 0.11 for SiMPL)
Extensive ablation studies: Systematic ablations in Sections 5.5 and Appendix E demonstrate importance of all components (B_off, P_Boff, B_on, π_exp)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations: Figure 1 provides intuitive understanding of skill refinement; Figure 7 shows progressive skill evolution; good use of trajectory visualizations
Strong reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters (Tables B.3-B.4), network architectures, full algorithm pseudocode, environment descriptions, supporting code availability
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core contributions (exploration near demonstrations, data prioritization, reward model relabeling) are straightforward applications of existing techniques; maximum return relabeling (Eq. 5) is simple max aggregation; dynamic β balancing uses standard Softmax; missing novel insights into why this combination works
Lack of theoretical analysis: No convergence guarantees, no characterization of when PRISM should outperform alternatives, missing analysis of noise propagation or failure modes

Questionable baseline fairness: PRISM refines skills during training while SiMPL/PEARL use fixed skills—a significant architectural advantage making direct comparison problematic; unclear if baselines were tuned for new environments (Office, AntMaze)

Method complexity with high hyperparameter burden: Multiple interacting components (π_exp, B_on, B_off prioritization, reward model, β, K_iter) with numerous hyperparameters (T, λ_kld_exp, β); periodic π_h reinitialization causes performance drops (Figure 6); no principled approach to setting hyperparameters a priori

Technical concerns inadequately addressed: (1) Reward model (Eq. 4) trained on meta-train data only—potential distribution shift on meta-test tasks; (2) max aggregation (Eq. 5) choice unjustified; (3) why this specific β formulation (Eq. 7)?; (4) buffer filtering criterion (Algorithm 1 Line 6) is overly permissive

Limited analysis of when PRISM helps: Marginal improvements in expert/low-noise regimes (Kitchen Expert: 17% gain); large gaps in high-noise (Office σ=0.3) suggest other factors; Maze2D σ=1.5 achieving 0.99 return counterintuitive; insufficient component attribution analysis

Statistical rigor concerns: Only 5 random seeds (top venues typically use 10+); overlapping confidence intervals in some comparisons; no significance testing; no wall-clock time comparisons despite acknowledged computational overhead from training both policies

Incomplete ablations and analysis: Missing ablations on K_iter sensitivity, fixed β performance, reward model training scope; task representation improvement (Fig. D.1) shown for Kitchen only; skill diversity/overlap not investigated

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear evidence (Fig. 2) that existing methods fail on noisy data
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 environments with systematic noise levels and extensive ablations
Consistent empirical improvements, particularly at high noise levels (e.g., Maze2D σ=1.5)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figs. 7, D.3) of skill refinement process
Extensive reproducibility effort with detailed hyperparameters and implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty: individual components (RND exploration, return-based prioritization, reward model relabeling) are standard techniques; combination is incremental

Key design choices lack principled justification: (a) Eq. 5 maximizing returns across all tasks unexplained, (b) Eq. 7 softmax balancing ad-hoc, (c) exploration 'near' offline data only loosely enforced through initialization

Unclear contribution of individual components: Fig. 8 shows PRISM w/o prioritization performs nearly identically, suggesting maximum return relabeling—claimed as key contribution—may be less critical than presented
Experimental setup differs from prior work: uses fewer tasks than SiMPL, resulting in lower baseline numbers on Maze2D Expert setup, undermining direct comparisons
No theoretical or intuitive justification for why reward models trained on exploration data should effectively relabel offline data from different distribution
Ablations don't isolate contributions: unclear how much improvement comes from (a) exploration, (b) online/offline balancing, or (c) specific maximum return relabeling
Reward model training (Eq. 4) only on high-return exploration data could introduce bias; no analysis of overfitting risk or failure modes
Non-uniform noise levels across environments (σ∈[0.1,0.3] vs [0.5,1.5]) makes cross-environment analysis inconsistent
Hyperparameter tuning question: environment-specific temperature T requires per-environment tuning, raising fair comparison concerns
Limited scope: only simulated D4RL environments; no robot experiments; no comparison to other noise-robust RL methods despite citing them in related work
Ad-hoc solutions: πh reinitialization every Kiter iterations addresses non-stationarity crudely; periodic performance drops visible in Fig. 6
Computational overhead acknowledged but downplayed; simultaneous training of three policies likely adds substantial cost not thoroughly analyzed

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an underexplored gap in skill-based meta-RL with noisy demonstrations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 environments with systematic noise level testing and 7 baselines
Strong and consistent empirical results, especially at high noise levels (e.g., Kitchen σ=0.3: 3.48 vs 0.81)
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating importance of each component
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and extensive implementation details supporting reproducibility
Detailed appendices providing network architectures, hyperparameters, and additional results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (exploration, reward models, prioritized sampling) without fundamental methodological innovations
Reward model reliability underexplored: trained on potentially limited data; no analysis of accuracy impact or failure modes
Fairness concerns with baselines: offline data collected from fewer tasks than SiMPL's original paper, making improvement attribution unclear
Significant hyperparameter sensitivity: temperature T requires per-environment tuning; λ_kld_exp varies with noise level, suggesting limited generalization
Lack of theoretical grounding: no convergence analysis or principled justification for maximum return relabeling over alternatives
Limited experimental scope: only Gaussian noise, synthetic demonstrations, simple environments (no vision-based control)
Modest improvements on high-quality data suggest benefits primarily for noisy scenarios rather than general improvements
Method complexity with multiple components (exploration policy, reward model, buffer management) increases implementation burden

strengths: Clear motivation and problem identification: Effectively demonstrates that existing skill-based meta-RL methods fail under noisy demonstrations (Fig. 2, Kitchen microwave example)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Four environments with systematic noise levels, additional stress tests (limited data, random injection, diverse sub-optimal data), thorough ablations
Strong and consistent empirical results: Improvements across all environments and noise levels, particularly impressive under high noise (Kitchen σ=0.3, Maze2D σ=1.5)
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed algorithms, extensive hyperparameters, code provided, clear implementation details across main paper and appendices
Good visualization and analysis: Effective illustrations of skill refinement dynamics (Figs. 7, F.2-F.3), buffer mixing coefficient evolution, task representation improvements
Practical relevance: Addresses real challenge in applying skill-based meta-RL to noisy real-world data
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Primarily combines existing techniques (decoupled policies, learned reward relabeling, RND exploration, SPiRL) without introducing fundamentally new ideas; contribution feels incremental

Experimental setup concerns: (1) Maze2D baseline discrepancy acknowledged—uses 40 tasks vs. more in SiMPL paper, results lower than reported; (2) Requires simple reward structures (subtask completion only) for reward model stability; (3) Different meta-test setup may favor SISL

Design choices lack principled justification: (1) Maximum return in Eq. 5 across all tasks unexplained—task-specific would be more natural; (2) Periodic refinement interval K_iter not ablated or justified; (3) Temperature parameter T requires environment-specific tuning (proportional to max return), somewhat ad-hoc

Computational overhead: 16% additional compute time during meta-training plus required meta-test fine-tuning; overhead justified only by claim that extended SiMPL training doesn't help, not by systematic budget-matched comparison
No theoretical analysis: Purely empirical contribution with no convergence guarantees, sample complexity analysis, or principled explanation of why this approach addresses noise robustness

Reward model limitations: (1) Trained only on online data (B_imp ∪ B_on), won't generalize to offline trajectories; (2) Table F.1 tests only on clean online data; (3) Restricted to simple reward structures

Scope limitations: (1) All experiments in simple visual environments with oracle policies; (2) No real robot experiments or complex visual RL benchmarks; (3) Kitchen environment uses only 4 rewards (one per subtask); (4) Scalability to complex reward functions not demonstrated

Missing important analyses: (1) Sensitivity to number of meta-training tasks; (2) Buffer transition dynamics (offline→online) not analyzed; (3) No systematic budget-matched comparison with baselines; (4) Performance scaling with dataset size

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear failure mode of existing methods (SiMPL, SPiRL) on noisy demonstrations, effectively illustrated through microwave opening task
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple environments with systematic noise injection and extensive ablation studies (components, hyperparameters, temperature, KLD coefficients)

Thorough documentation with detailed appendices including implementation details, network architectures, additional visualizations, and robustness tests (limited data, random noise injection, sub-optimal datasets)
Consistent empirical improvements over SiMPL baseline across multiple environments and noise levels, with particularly strong results under high noise regimes
Effective visualizations showing skill refinement progression, buffer mixing dynamics, t-SNE of learned skill structures, and task representation improvements
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: decoupled exploration/exploitation policies are standard, RND-based exploration is conventional, reward model prioritization is straightforward; the contribution is primarily combining these existing techniques for this specific setting rather than novel methodology

Unfair baseline comparison: authors acknowledge SiMPL's reported results differ from their implementation due to different data collection procedures (40 vs. more tasks), undermining direct comparison of relative improvements

Insufficient analysis of mechanisms: paper demonstrates SISL works but doesn't deeply explain why, which components matter most (only shows all-or-nothing ablations), or how much improvement comes from clean online rewards vs. reward model prioritization

High complexity and computational overhead: framework requires three separate buffers, periodic skill refinement every K_iter, multiple new hyperparameters (T, λ^kld_imp), and adds 16% computational cost; meta-test fine-tuning is required for optimal performance, reducing practical appeal

Limited experimental scope: all environments have discrete subtask structure (Kitchen, Office) or simple goal-reaching (Maze2D, AntMaze); no continuous control tasks without subtask labels, no real robotics, no comparison with noise-robust methods from imitation learning

Questionable design choices lack justification: periodic rather than continuous skill refinement, max operator in Eq. 5 for computing hypothetical returns, dynamic β computation assumes task-independent return scales; ablations show re-initialization is necessary but don't justify why periodic refinement is needed
Artificial noise model: main experiments use only Gaussian action noise; real-world degradation (systematic bias, sensor failures) is underexplored, limiting applicability claims

Incomplete analysis of key components: reward model trained on clean online data only (not affected by offline noise) suggests improvements may come from access to clean signals rather than prioritization specifically; no ablation isolating reward model contribution vs. exploration policy contribution

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: robustness to noisy demonstrations in skill-based meta-RL
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 4 environments, multiple noise levels, thorough ablations, and diverse robustness tests
Consistent improvements over baselines across settings, with particularly strong results under high-noise regimes
Clear methodology and good presentation with informative visualizations and extensive reproducibility information
Practical relevance to real-world scenarios where clean demonstrations are expensive
Thorough appendix with detailed implementation, additional experiments, and analysis of the refinement process
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (decoupled exploration, return relabeling, RND) without introducing fundamentally new concepts
No theoretical justification or convergence analysis; lacks principled explanation for why this particular combination works
Experimental setup concerns: Maze2D uses fewer tasks than SiMPL during offline data generation, resulting in weaker baselines and inflated improvements
Multiple hyperparameters with significant sensitivity (T, λ^kld_imp, K_iter) requiring domain knowledge for tuning despite provided guidelines
Insufficient comparison with recent work: baselines are from 2021-2022 and limited discussion of recent offline-RL methods
Requires meta-test fine-tuning unlike pure meta-RL methods, increasing computational cost and reducing true meta-learning capability
Reward model training assumes access to clean task rewards; insufficient analysis of robustness to reward misspecification or poor early-training quality
~16% computational overhead during meta-training; limited analysis of actual wall-clock time and scalability implications
Task-specific improvement policies introduce memory overhead proportional to number of training tasks; scalability concerns unaddressed
Limited environment diversity: all tasks are relatively simple; Office and AntMaze newly introduced but not extensively validated
